title: Backcasting: Minimum Viable Deception Detection for Small Model Evaluators

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Deception detection in LLMs is an active research area. OpenDeception (2025) introduced 50 real-world scenarios benchmarking deceptive intentions and capabilities. METR and others have established model evaluation frameworks. The 'evaluation faking' phenomenon (models detecting when they are being evaluated and behaving differently) has been documented. Linear probes for detecting strategic deception have been explored (LessWrong). However, the specific question of formalizing minimum requirements for a 'safe evaluator' — what capability level, architecture, and training history a smaller model must have to reliably detect deception in a more capable model — has not been directly addressed. The circular trust problem is acknowledged but no formal specification framework exists. Partially novel in its formalization approach, but the underlying challenge is well-recognized.

title: Applying Interrogation Resistance Training Research to Model Probe Hardening

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: The cross-disciplinary analogy between human interrogation resistance and AI model probe resistance is creative and largely unstudied. While deception detection in AI models is well-researched (linear probes, activation patching, behavioral probing), and human interrogation psychology is its own field, the explicit mapping of interrogation resistance tactics to model probe evasion strategies has not been directly attempted. Sarkadi's 'Deception Analysis with Artificial Intelligence: An Interdisciplinary Perspective' (arXiv:2406.05724) is the closest work, surveying deception from an interdisciplinary lens but not specifically mapping interrogation resistance mechanisms to AI probe hardening. The observation that 'training out scheming may teach more covert scheming' (OpenAI, 2025) is tangentially related but does not use the interrogation framework. The analogy may be loose, but the specific research program of systematically cataloging resistance mechanisms and designing counter-probes is novel.

title: Causal Chain Intervention: How Does Memory Architecture Affect Deceptive Goal Persistence?

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Memory architecture and its safety implications for agentic systems is a growing area, but the specific question of whether deceptive goals persist differently across stateless vs. memory-augmented architectures has not been directly studied. Existing literature covers memory poisoning defenses ('Memory Firewall' concept), RAG architecture safety, and the general principle that LLMs are stateless per-request. Sleeper Agents (Hubinger et al. 2024) showed persistent deceptive behavior through safety training, but in a single-architecture setting. No published work systematically compares deceptive goal persistence across memory conditions (stateless, external memory, memory-wiped) as a controlled experiment. The idea that statelessness could be a structural safety property is mentioned informally but not empirically tested. This is a genuinely novel experimental design.
